554.title: Peace on the messengers
554.hook: glory to your Lord, peace on the messengers, praise to Allah (37:180–182)
554.howItsDone: Many Muslims recite the last three verses of As-Saffat (37:180–182) to close a lesson, a gathering or a prayer, and send peace on the prophets whenever they are named.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Yunus again, and your line was glorifying got him out. Did you practice a little glorifying while nothing was wrong? Today, the last three verses of As-Saffat. Day five hundred fifty-four.

Some songs have a refrain you start waiting for. The verse changes, the story moves on, and then the chorus comes back and you can almost sing it before it arrives. Surah As-Saffat has one. It tells story after story of prophets, and after several of them the same short line returns, like a bell: peace be on him. And then, at the very end, the refrain opens up to include every messenger at once, and the surah closes with three lines some Muslims use to close a gathering.

Go back through As-Saffat and listen for it. After Nuh's story: peace be on Nuh among the worlds. After Ibrahim's: peace be on Ibrahim. After Musa and Harun's: peace be on Musa and Harun. After Ilyas: peace be on Il-yasin. Each time, the Arabic begins salamun 'ala, peace upon. Four of the stories end that way, in peace, however hard they were. Then, the surah's last three verses. First: glory to your Lord, the Lord of might, above what they describe. In the verse, that clears away every wrong picture of Allah. Second, Pickthall: "And peace be unto those sent (to warn). And praise be to Allah, Lord of the Worlds!" Now the refrain isn't for one prophet. It's for all of them, the named and the unnamed, everyone ever sent. And the last word goes back to the opening of al-Fatiha: al-hamdu lillahi rabbi'l-'alamin, praise be to Allah, Lord of the Worlds. So the surah ends with three moves: glory, peace, praise. Glory says what Allah is above. Peace blesses those who carried His message. Praise says where everything belongs. Commentators, including Ibn Kathir, mention an early saying that whoever wants their reward measured out in full should end their gathering with these verses. Its chain is discussed. Some Muslims recite them at the end of a lesson, a dinner, a meeting. Ending a conversation by wishing peace on every messenger who ever lived is not a bad way to leave a room.
screen: `PRAISE TO THE LORD OF THE WORLDS.`

segments.voice: Today's practice is to end the day with these three, so rehearse them now. Sit and breathe. On one breath, think glory: the verse says God is beyond whatever is pictured. On the next, think peace: on every messenger, every person who ever carried something true to people who didn't want it. On the next, think praise: where everything belongs. If you pray, you can say the three verses in Arabic or in your own language. Then rest. The bell holds the time.
Peace on the messengers. As-Saffat's refrain, peace upon each prophet, which at the end widens to all of them, between glory and praise. Today's word.
Your line: peace on the messengers. Tonight, before you sleep, or at the end of a gathering, close with the three: glory, peace, praise. Day five hundred fifty-four.

555.title: Dawud and the two brothers
555.hook: two men climb the wall with a dispute over ewes, and Dawud realizes he was tested and repents (38:21–25)
555.howItsDone: Many Muslims perform a prostration of recitation (sajdat al-tilawa) at 38:24; schools differ on whether it is required or recommended, and Islamic legal teaching stresses hearing both parties before judging.

segments.voice: Yesterday, peace on the messengers, and your line was the same. Did you close the day with glory, peace and praise? Today, a new surah, and Dawud again, this time as a judge. Day five hundred fifty-five.

It's a private hour. Dawud is in his prayer chamber, and the commentators say no one was to come in. Then two men come over the wall. Not through the door. Over the wall. He's startled, and you can feel it in the text: he's afraid. They say, quickly, don't be afraid. We're two parties in a dispute; one of us has wronged the other. Judge between us with truth, and don't be unjust, and guide us to the right path. Then one of them tells his story, and Dawud answers before the text gives the other one a word.

Surah Sad, verse twenty-three. The first man says: this is my brother. He has ninety-nine ewes, and I have one ewe. And he said, give it to me, and he overpowered me in argument. Ninety-nine and one. It's built to provoke. And Dawud says, right away: he has wronged you by asking to add your ewe to his. Many partners wrong one another, except those who believe and do good, and how few they are. Then verse twenty-four, the turn. Dawud realized that We had tested him. And he asked his Lord for forgiveness, fell down bowing, and turned back in repentance. What was the test? The Qur'an doesn't say, and commentators differ. Some later stories, known as Isra'iliyyat, tie it to an episode about another man's wife; many Muslim scholars, Ibn Kathir among them, set those stories aside, holding that prophets are protected from such a sin. A reading many find more convincing stays inside the scene: Dawud ruled after hearing only one side. The text never gives the second man a word. The story was perfectly built to make him judge fast, and he did. And the moment he saw it, he didn't defend himself. He went down on his face. Verse twenty-six gives the lesson to him directly: O Dawud, We have made you a successor on earth, so judge between people with truth, and don't follow desire. Many Muslims prostrate when they recite verse twenty-four. A hadith in Bukhari reports that Ibn 'Abbas saw the Prophet ﷺ prostrate there.
screen: `HE KNEW HE WAS TESTED, AND BOWED.`

segments.voice: The practice: reconsider a judgment you made. Sit and settle. Bring to mind one recent judgment, about a coworker, a relative, someone online, where you heard one side and decided. Now give the other side a voice. What might they say, if they got to speak? You don't have to change your mind. Just let the second man talk. Notice how it feels to hold the judgment a little more loosely. The bell holds the time.
Dawud and the two brothers. A dispute over ninety-nine ewes and one, a quick ruling, and a prophet who saw he'd been tested and bowed in repentance. Today's word.
screen: `DAWUD AND THE TWO BROTHERS — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: judge, then look at yourself. Today, before you pass a verdict on anyone, ask one question: have I heard the other side? Day five hundred fifty-five.

556.title: Ayyub's spring
556.hook: strike the ground with your foot: a cool spring to wash and drink (38:41–44)
556.howItsDone: Muslims hold up Ayyub as the model of sabr, patience in illness and loss; his cry in 21:83 is often recited by the sick, and his story is told to comfort those in long hardship.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Dawud and the two brothers, and your line was judge, then look at yourself. Did you give the other side a voice before deciding? Day five hundred fifty-six.

A hot afternoon, years of illness behind you, your body aching, and someone hands you a glass of cold water. You drink it slowly. Then you splash some on your face, the back of your neck, your wrists. For a moment, that's everything. Back in Surah Al-Anbiya, we heard Ayyub's cry: harm has touched me, and You are the most merciful. Surah Sad tells what happened next, and the answer to years of suffering arrives in the most ordinary form there is. Water. Under his own feet.

Surah Sad, verse forty-one. Remember Our servant Ayyub, when he called his Lord: Satan has touched me with weariness and torment. Then verse forty-two, the answer, as a command: urkud bi-rijlik, strike the ground with your foot. And there it is: a spring. Cool water to wash in, and to drink. Notice that he has to do something. Not much. One stamp of a weak foot. But the healing comes through that small act, and through water, the plainest gift of all. Verse forty-three: and We gave him back his family, and as many again with them, a mercy from Us and a reminder for those with understanding. Then a stranger detail. Verse forty-four: take a bundle of grass in your hand and strike with it, and don't break your oath. Commentators explain that during his illness Ayyub had sworn to strike someone, many say his wife, a set number of times. Allah gave him a gentle way to keep his word without harming her: one tap with a bundle of stalks. Mercy for him, and mercy for her. And then the verdict: We found him patient. How excellent a servant! He was always turning back. There's a hadith in Bukhari that adds one more picture. After his healing, while Ayyub was bathing, a shower of golden locusts fell, and he began gathering them. His Lord called: didn't I make you rich enough? And Ayyub answered: yes, but I can never do without Your blessing. Patient in the long hardship, and still grateful for every small gift after it.
screen: `A COOL SPRING TO WASH AND DRINK.`
`A BUNDLE OF GRASS, AN OATH KEPT.`

segments.voice: The practice: wash your face with cool water. If you can, go to a sink now. Let the water run cold. Cup it in your hands, and wash your face slowly, once, twice, three times. Feel it on your forehead, your eyes, your cheeks. If you can't get up, picture it in detail. Then sit, damp-faced, and think of Ayyub's spring: the answer to years of waiting, in the plainest gift there is. The bell holds the time.
Ayyub's spring. After long illness, Ayyub is told to strike the ground with his foot, and a cool spring rises for washing and drinking. Today's word.

Your line: patient; a spring came. Today, when something has been hard for a long time, take one small step, one stamp of the foot, and watch for the ordinary gift that answers. Day five hundred fifty-six.

557.title: Iblis asks for time
557.hook: Iblis refuses again and asks for respite to mislead, except the sincere (38:71–83)
557.howItsDone: Muslims speak of ikhlas, sincerity, as doing every act for Allah alone, and many renew their intention (niyya) before prayer, charity and other good deeds.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ayyub's spring, and your line was patient; a spring came. Did you take one small step on something long and hard? Today, the end of Surah Sad. Day five hundred fifty-seven.

This path has met this scene before: Adam made from clay, the angels told to bow, and one who refused. Iblis, saying I'm better than him, You made me from fire and him from clay. Back on day twenty-four, the lesson was pride. Surah Sad tells the scene again, and lets it run a few lines further, past the refusal, into a negotiation. Iblis, expelled, doesn't beg to come back. He asks for something else. Time. And in his own boast, he admits there's someone he can't touch.

Verses seventy-one to seventy-six give the refusal: I am better than him. Then seventy-seven and seventy-eight: go out from here, you are rejected, and My curse is on you until the Day of Judgment. Verse seventy-nine. Iblis says: my Lord, then give me respite until the day they are raised. Notice two things. He still says my Lord. He doesn't deny Allah exists; he refuses Him. And he doesn't ask for forgiveness. He asks for time, to use against the people he refused to bow to. Allah answers: you are of those given respite, until the day of the known time. Then the boast, verse eighty-two and eighty-three. He swears by Allah's own might that he'll mislead every one of them. And then he adds the exception himself. Pickthall: "Save Thy single-minded slaves among them." The Arabic is al-mukhlasin, those made sincere, purified. The word is recited two ways in the established readings of the Qur'an. Mukhlasin, those Allah has made sincere. And mukhlisin, those who make their worship sincere. Some scholars hold both meanings at once: sincerity is something a person works at, and something given. Either way, the enemy names his own limit. He can whisper to anyone. He can't take someone whose devotion is single-minded, done for Allah alone, not for an audience. The surah closes soon after with the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ told to say: I ask no payment for this, and I'm not one who pretends. Sincerity, at the start and at the end.

The practice: do one thing sincerely. Sit, and choose one small thing you'll do today: a kindness, a task, a prayer if you pray. Now look at the reason you're doing it. Is part of it for someone to notice? Gently set that part down. Imagine doing it with no one ever knowing, only God, or only you. See how it feels, lighter or harder. Rest there. The bell holds the time.
Iblis asks for time. Expelled, he asks for respite until the Day to mislead people, and names his own exception: the sincere. Today's word.
Your line: the sincere are protected. Today, do the one thing you chose, and don't tell anyone you did it. Day five hundred fifty-seven.

558.title: Are they equal?
558.hook: are those who know and those who don't know equal (39:9)
558.carry: knowing isn't equal to not knowing
558.howItsDone: Muslims treat seeking knowledge as a religious duty; many attend study circles (halaqas) at mosques, and 39:9 is quoted to encourage study.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Iblis asks for time, and your line was the sincere are protected. Did you do one thing today that nobody will ever hear about? Today, a new surah, Az-Zumar. Day five hundred fifty-eight.

Some questions don't need an answer. Is a full glass heavier than an empty one? Would you rather be warm or freezing? A teacher asks one in class and nobody raises a hand, because the answer is sitting right there in the question. The Qur'an asks questions like this, and Surah Az-Zumar, the thirty-ninth, has one about knowing. You might expect it to start in a classroom. It starts in the middle of the night.
screen: `IT STARTS IN THE MIDDLE OF THE NIGHT.`

segments.voice: Verse nine opens with a picture. Someone is up in the hours of the night, prostrating and standing in prayer, wary of the hereafter, hoping for the mercy of their Lord. Is that person like the one who isn't? Then the famous line. Pickthall: "Are those who know equal with those who know not? But only men of understanding will pay heed." The answer is built in: no. But look at what knowing means here. It's not trivia. It sits right after the night prayer, the fear, the hope. Some commentators read the knowing in this verse as knowing your Lord and acting on it: the person who knows why they're awake in the night. So the verse sets learning and devotion side by side. And the tradition took that seriously. A hadith in Sahih Muslim says that whoever walks a path seeking knowledge, Allah makes easy for them a path to paradise. Another, in Ibn Majah, says seeking knowledge is an obligation on every Muslim, and scholars point out that this includes men and women alike. Then the last phrase: only people of understanding, ulu'l-albab, will take it to heart. Albab is the plural of lubb, a kernel, the inner core of a nut. People of understanding are people who get to the core of things. Knowing and not knowing aren't the same. But the verse adds: it takes some knowing even to notice that.
screen: `A PATH TO KNOWLEDGE, A PATH TO PARADISE.`

segments.voice: Ten minutes of reading starts with one page. If you have a book nearby, a Qur'an, a history, anything worth learning from, open it and read one page slowly, as if you'll be asked about it. If not, think of one subject you've always meant to understand better, and choose the first thing you'll read about it. Then sit with what you read, or what you chose, and let it settle to its kernel. The bell holds the time.
Are they equal? Surah Az-Zumar's question: are those who know equal to those who don't, asked right after a picture of someone praying at night. Today's word.
Your line: knowing isn't equal to not knowing. Today, find ten minutes, and read something that makes you know a little more than this morning. Day five hundred fifty-eight.

559.title: Don't despair
559.hook: O My servants who have wronged yourselves, don't despair of Allah's mercy, He forgives all sins (39:53)
559.howItsDone: Muslims seek forgiveness by saying astaghfirullah, often many times a day, and many scholars and preachers quote 39:53 to people who feel their sins are too great to be forgiven.

segments.voice: Yesterday, are they equal, and your line was knowing isn't equal to not knowing. Did you find ten minutes to read? Day five hundred fifty-nine.

A group of men come to the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ. They've done terrible things: killed many times, and committed adultery many times. They've listened to his message, and they like it. But they have one problem, and they say it straight. What you're calling us to is good. If only you could tell us there's a way to make up for what we've done. They aren't arguing. They're asking whether it's already too late. A report in Sahih al-Bukhari says the answer came as revelation, and one of the verses was this one.

Surah Az-Zumar, verse fifty-three. Pickthall: "Say: O My slaves who have been prodigal to their own hurt! Despair not of the mercy of Allah, Who forgiveth all sins. Lo! He is the Forgiving, the Merciful." Start with the address. Ya 'ibadiya, O My servants. Before a word about what they did, Allah calls them His. People who have gone too far, the Arabic says, against their own souls, and they're still addressed as Mine. And the first command isn't to do this or that. It's: don't despair. La taqnatu. The verb names the despair of someone who has stopped expecting anything. The verse forbids that before it promises anything else. Then the promise: He forgives all sins, jami'an, every one of them. Scholars read this together with the very next verse, which says: turn to your Lord and submit to Him before the punishment comes. So the door is wide, and the way through it is turning back. Some early authorities are reported to have called it the most hopeful verse in the Qur'an. And notice who it was for. Not people with small slips, but men who had killed. Teachers draw the point out: if the verse reached them, it reaches the person who skipped their prayers for a month, or broke a promise, or fell back into an old habit. In that reading, the danger isn't only the mistake. It's deciding the mistake is the end.

The practice: come back after a lapse. Sit, and think of one good habit you let slip: a prayer, a walk, a call to a parent, this very path if you missed some days. Notice any voice saying it's too late, or you always do this. Hear the verse's first words instead: O My servants. Then decide the smallest way to come back today. Not to make up for everything. Just to return. If you pray, you can say astaghfirullah. The bell holds the time.
Don't despair. Az-Zumar fifty-three: to people who have wronged themselves, never lose hope in Allah's mercy, for He forgives all sins to those who turn back. Today's word.
Your line: never despair of mercy. Today, pick up the habit you let slip, even for one minute, without making up for the gap. Day five hundred fifty-nine.

560.title: Led in groups
560.hook: the mindful are led to the garden in groups, and greeted with peace (39:73)
560.tomorrow: Forgiver of sin, accepter of return
560.howItsDone: Muslims greet one another with as-salamu 'alaykum, peace be upon you, the same greeting the Qur'an says the angels give at the garden's gates, and are encouraged to keep good company.

segments.voice: Yesterday, don't despair, and your line was never despair of mercy. Did you pick up something you'd let slip? Today ends the week and Surah Az-Zumar. Day five hundred sixty.

Watch the doors of a wedding hall, a stadium, a graduation. People rarely arrive alone. They come in clusters: a family, a carload of friends, a team in matching shirts. You can tell who belongs with whom by who they're walking beside. Surah thirty-nine is named for that. Zumar: groups, crowds, companies. And at its very end, it pictures the Day of Judgment not as a long line of individuals, but as people arriving in groups, and the gates they arrive at.

Verse seventy-one: those who denied are driven toward hell in groups, and when they arrive, its gates are opened, and its keepers ask: didn't messengers come to you? Verse seventy-three: those who were mindful of their Lord are led to the garden in groups. When they arrive, and its gates have been opened, its keepers say: salamun 'alaykum, peace be upon you. You've done well, so enter, to stay. Now a small detail in the Arabic. In the first verse, when they arrive, its gates are opened, futihat. In the second, there's an extra and: wa futihat, and its gates have been opened. Some commentators read that and as meaning the garden's gates were already open, waiting for them, like a host who unlocks the door before guests reach the house. And look at the first words: peace. Not a test, not a question. A greeting. Elsewhere the Qur'an says each person comes to Him alone; here, at the gates, they arrive together. Then verse seventy-four: the people say, praise be to Allah, who has fulfilled His promise to us. And the surah ends with the angels circling the Throne, and the words: praise be to Allah, Lord of the Worlds. Look back across this week and you'll see the same arc: peace on all the messengers; Dawud bowing when he saw his mistake; Ayyub's spring after long illness; the sincere that Iblis can't reach; the one who prays at night and knows; mercy for those who'd gone too far. And now groups of people, walking together toward open gates, greeted with peace.
screen: `PRAISE TO THE LORD OF THE WORLDS.`

segments.voice: The practice: walk with good people. Sit, and think of the people you spend most of your time with. Picture them as a group walking somewhere together. Which way are they walking? Who leaves you steadier than they found you? Hold one of them in mind. If you pray, thank God for them; if not, simply be grateful. Then think of one person you'd like to walk with more often. The bell holds the time.
Led in groups. Az-Zumar's last scene: the mindful led to the garden together, the gates already open, greeted with peace. Today's word.
Your line: greeted with peace. Today, greet the people you walk with first, before they greet you, and mean it. Day five hundred sixty, and the end of the week.

wa futihat: like a host who opens the door before the guests arrive.

fork.setup: the mindful arrive at the garden in groups. the gates are open. what do the keepers say first?
fork.reveal: peace be upon you. you've done well, so enter, to stay.

original.note: Arabic: in groups, in companies, the word that names surah thirty-nine.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Day is only about standing alone.
what it means: Az-Zumar pictures people led in groups, and the garden's gates open with a greeting of peace.

what a scholar hears: 19:95 has each one coming alone, while 39:71–73 has them arriving zumar; 39:71 has futihat, 39:73 wa futihat; some tafsir read the added waw as the gates already open, honoring the arrivals.

sources.ref: tafsir on 39:73 (the waw in wa futihat)
